findings.title: `queued` default is evaluated once at import time, not per instance
findings.body: The dataclass field `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` captures the timestamp at module import time, so every `AssignmentSource` created via `from_integration()` or `from_dict()` without an explicit `queued` value gets the same process-start timestamp instead of the time the assignment change actually occurred. The field is serialized via `to_dict()` into the `sync_assignee_outbound` task kwargs, so any use of `queued` for observability, debugging, or staleness checks will be silently wrong. The fix is `queued: datetime = field(default_factory=timezone.now)`. The new unit test (`test_to_dict`) only asserts `queued is not None`, so it passes despite the bug.

findings.title: Base `should_sync` signature widened positionally but no provider subclasses were updated
findings.body: `IssueSyncIntegration.should_sync` now takes a second positional argument `sync_source`, and `sync_assignee_outbound` (the task) calls `installation.should_sync("outbound_assignee", parsed_assignment_source)` with two positional arguments. The PR changes no provider integration files (Jira, VSTS, GitLab, etc.). Any integration subclass that overrides `should_sync(self, attribute)` with the old single-parameter signature (the pattern this PR itself uses for the base-class override pair in this file) will raise `TypeError: should_sync() takes 2 positional arguments but 3 were given` inside the task, causing the assignee sync task to fail and retry for that provider. Every override in the codebase must be updated or verified to accept the extra argument before merging.

findings.title: `assignment_source` plumbed into `sync_status_outbound` signature but never passed by any caller
findings.body: The abstract method `sync_status_outbound` gained an `assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None` parameter, but no call site anywhere in this PR (or the changed task) passes `assignment_source` to `sync_status_outbound`, and no implementation was updated to consume it. Since the PR is titled "Breaks issue sync cycles" and status sync is part of the same inbound-webhook/outbound-update loop described in the issue, this is incomplete plumbing: status sync cycles are not actually prevented, and the parameter is dead code that suggests protection that does not exist.

findings.title: Cycle suppression is per-integration, dropping syncs to sibling linked issues of the same integration
findings.body: In `sync_group_assignee_outbound`, the `AssignmentSource` only carries `integration_id`, and `should_sync` suppresses the outbound sync for every external issue belonging to the source integration. When a Sentry group is linked to multiple external issues from the same integration (multiple GroupLink rows referencing different ExternalIssues of one integration), an inbound webhook from one of those issues now silently prevents the assignee change from propagating to the other linked issues of that integration — a behavior regression from before, where each linked issue was updated. Carrying the triggering external issue id in `AssignmentSource` would scope the suppression correctly.

findings.title: `from_dict` fails open and does not validate the `queued` type
findings.body: `from_dict` returns `None` on `ValueError`/`TypeError`, and `sync_assignee_outbound` then proceeds with `assignment_source=None`, which re-enables the outbound sync — i.e., the exact sync-cycle bug this PR fixes silently returns if the dict is malformed. Additionally, a dict where `queued` is a string (e.g., after a JSON round-trip through the broker, since `to_dict()` emits a `datetime`) is accepted without complaint, producing an `AssignmentSource` whose `queued` field holds a string rather than a datetime. At minimum the `queued` value should be parsed/validated, and the fail-open behavior should be logged so operators can detect when cycle protection is being bypassed.

findings.title: No test that other integrations still receive the outbound sync when a source is set
findings.body: The PR's stated goal is that suppressing the sync to the originating integration "should still allow other integrations to propagate changes outward," but there is no test for that path. `test_assignee_sync_outbound_assign_with_matching_source_integration` only covers the suppression case (single integration, `assert_not_called`). A test with two linked integrations (source = integration A, asserting integration B's `sync_assignee_outbound` is still called with the assignment source) is needed to lock in the cross-integration propagation behavior and to catch regressions where the suppression is over-broad. There is also no end-to-end test of `sync_group_assignee_inbound` producing an `AssignmentSource` that suppresses the echo through the real task path.
